blocks.text: With this unity begins the systematic study of the Egyptian of Cairo, the variety chosen as the first dialect (A2-24, decision form). In A2-23 you have learned to recognize him; Now learn how to use it in your daily talk. The EGY track takes about a quarter of your study time, in blocks separated by fuṣḥā: a block is eitherfuṣḥāNever the two things together. In this first unit activate the sounds of Cairo, greetings with their obligated answers, pronouns and phrases to present yourself and ask for help when you don't understand. Six weeks, in parallel with B1-01 and B1-02.

rows: A2-23 (recognition of the Egyptian); decision on registered dialect
8–9 hours · six weeks (weeks 95–100), about 1,5 hours per week in two blocks

blocks.text: Materials This unit, a tutor or Egyptian conversation partner, tutor recordings on the phone
Targets. At the end of the unit you know:
1. the sounds of Cairo (g, ʾ instead of q, ē, ō, t e d in place of ṯ and ḏ);
2. greeting and responding with the right formula, to a man and a woman;
3. to present yourself: name, origin, where you live, what you do;
4. ask the same questions to another person;
5. manage the misunderstanding: ask to repeat, to speak slowly, what a word means.
Six-week plan (two blocks from 40–45 minutes per week).

What changes compared to A2-23. In A2 you recognized the Egyptian and led him back to fuṣḥā. Now you talk to him: answer, ask questions, manage everyday situations. The fuṣḥā remains the language of reading and writing the course. As we write the Egyptian. In the dialogues the Egyptian is written as the Egyptians write it in the messages and subtitles: Arabic letters, almost without vowels, with the same conventions of fuṣḥā (the ⁧ق⁩ stays ⁧ق⁩ even if you read ʾ; the ⁧ج⁩ stays ⁧ج⁩ even if you read g). Transliteration is the guide to pronunciation: read it always together with Arabic. In your written exercises respond to transliteration; If you want, add the Arabic spelling. The Egyptian transliteration. As in A2-23: g per ⁧ج⁩ , ʾ for the hamza (even when it comes from ⁧ق⁩ ), ē and ō for long vowels born from ay and aw, double consonants written twice. The article is the- and assimilates to solar letters as in fuṣḥā (iš-šaraf, it-talāt). Rules against interference (A2-24): separate study blocks; in the notebook, separate pages with the label [EGY]; when you write an email or a theme, always fuṣḥā. The Egyptian is not "fuṣḥā wrong: it is another variety, with its own and consistent rules.

chapters.title: 8. The phrases to not get lost

blocks.text: The rhythm. The Egyptian shortens many vowels and drops some of them: ʿalā → ʿala, fī → fi; in front of two consonants rests a short vowel: w-inta, wi-sākin. Don't pronounce case terminations. The accent. It often falls to a different point from fuṣḥā: madrása (fuṣḥā mádrasa), ʾahwa. Do not look for rules now: repeat the phrases of the dialogue after the tutor, imitating melody and accent, and record. Shadowing. The tutor reads a line of dialogue 1; You repeat it right after, overlapping his voice three times. Then without reading.
